Hear a black hole merger

Real data from the LIGO Livingston detector, turned into sound. Use headphones if you can: the chirps are deep, and laptop speakers struggle below about 100 Hz.

Why does the pitch rise?

Two black holes orbiting each other send out gravitational waves, ripples in space itself. The waves go up and down twice per orbit, so their pitch is twice the orbit rate. The waves carry energy away, so the black holes sink closer together. Closer orbits are faster orbits (just as Mercury goes around the Sun faster than Earth), so the pitch goes up. Faster orbits lose energy even faster, so it runs away: the pitch sweeps upward more and more quickly until the two black holes touch and merge. That rising "whoop" is called a chirp.

Mass sets the sound. Heavy black holes are big, so they touch while still orbiting fairly slowly: the chirp ends at a low pitch and is over almost instantly (GW190521). Light ones can get much closer before touching, so they orbit faster and spend longer in LIGO's hearing range: a longer chirp that climbs higher (GW190814).

The white dashed line on each picture is the textbook prediction, worked out from Einstein's equations in their simplest form, using the masses LIGO measured. It's not fitted to the picture, yet it follows the bright track. It's not perfect: it is the simplest version of the formula (it's least accurate for very unequal masses, like GW190814), it fails in the last instant when the two objects touch, and GWOSC's merger times are rounded to 0.1 s, so the curve can sit a few hundredths of a second off.

What you hear is mostly noise: the data were "whitened" (noise at every pitch made equally loud) and filtered to 25–400 Hz. Listen for the short upward "whoop" about two seconds in, over the hiss. For GW190521 it's only a low thump.

Data: Gravitational Wave Open Science Center (GWOSC), gwosc.org: 32 s of LIGO Livingston strain data around each event, with masses, distances and merger times from the GWOSC event catalog (GWTC-1 and GWTC-2.1). *Distances are "luminosity distances", worked out from how faint the signal is. For far-away events this is larger than the distance the waves actually travelled, because the Universe expanded while they were on their way. This research has made use of data or software obtained from GWOSC, a service of the LIGO Scientific Collaboration, the Virgo Collaboration, and KAGRA.

Made with gwpy, matplotlib and scipy for CS85. Code: project19/make_gallery.py.
